headline: Diphtheria Immunization in Schools
source: American Journal of Public Health and the Nation's Health (via PubMed Central)
blurb: A one-page item in a public health journal from March 1928 about giving diphtheria shots in schools.

headline: Progress Report on Pertussis Immunization
source: American Journal of Public Health and the Nation's Health (via PubMed Central)
blurb: Pearl Kendrick and Grace Eldering reported on their whooping cough immunization work in a paper first read to the American Public Health Association in October 1935.

headline: Active Immunization Against Poliomyelitis
source: American Journal of Public Health and the Nation's Health (via PubMed Central)
blurb: Maurice Brodie and William H. Park published a paper on immunizing people against polio, first read at a public health meeting in St. Louis in November 1935.

headline: Simultaneous Administration of Diphtheria Toxoid and Pertussis Vaccine in Young Children
source: American Journal of Public Health and the Nation's Health (via PubMed Central)
blurb: Louis W. Sauer and Winston H. Tucker published a paper on giving young children diphtheria and whooping cough shots at the same time.

headline: Current Status of Immunization Procedures—A Symposium: Pertussis
source: American Journal of Public Health and the Nation's Health (via PubMed Central)
blurb: Joseph A. Bell reviewed where whooping cough vaccination stood, in a talk given to the American Public Health Association in October 1947.

headline: Historical Vaccine Concerns
source: CDC
blurb: In 1955, some batches of polio vaccine from Cutter Laboratories contained live polio virus, more than 250 polio cases were tied to them, and the vaccine was recalled.

headline: Jonas Salk and the Polio Vaccine
source: Dwight D. Eisenhower Presidential Library
blurb: On April 12, 1955, Americans got the news that Dr. Jonas Salk had developed a polio vaccine, and the federal government set up a plan to have six licensed companies make it for children across the country.

headline: Statement by the President on the Polio Vaccine Situation.
source: The American Presidency Project, UC Santa Barbara
blurb: President Eisenhower said a committee of scientists was screening polio vaccine before release, that more than 5.5 million children had been vaccinated, and how the vaccine would be shared out.

headline: The Polio Vaccine Assistance Act of 1955
source: American Journal of Public Health and the Nation's Health (via PubMed Central)
blurb: Otis L. Anderson wrote a two-page article in a public health journal about the 1955 federal law on polio vaccine.

headline: Dr. Albert Sabin: A Closer Look
source: National Library of Medicine, Circulating Now
blurb: In 1961, the U.S. Public Health Service approved Albert Sabin's polio vaccine, which was given by mouth and became the preferred polio vaccine in the United States.

headline: Public Law 87-868
source: U.S. Statutes at Large, 76 Stat. 1155 (govinfo.gov)
blurb: The Vaccination Assistance Act of 1962 set aside federal money to help states and communities run vaccination programs against polio, diphtheria, whooping cough, and tetanus, with a focus on preschool children.

headline: History of Measles
source: CDC
blurb: In 1963, John Enders and colleagues turned a strain of the measles virus into a vaccine that was licensed in the United States.

headline: Impact of U.S. MMR Vaccination Program
source: CDC
blurb: During the last major U.S. rubella epidemic, from 1964 to 1965, an estimated 12.5 million people got rubella and about 20,000 babies were born with congenital rubella syndrome.

headline: Epidemiologic basis for eradication of measles in 1967
source: Public Health Reports (via PubMed Central)
blurb: D. J. Sencer, H. B. Dull, and A. D. Langmuir published a paper in Public Health Reports on the basis for wiping out measles in 1967.

headline: Surveillance of mumps in the United States as background for use of vaccine
source: Public Health Reports (via PubMed Central)
blurb: J. J. Witte and A. W. Karchmer published a report on how mumps cases were tracked in the United States, written as background for using the mumps vaccine.

headline: Vaccine History: Developments by Year
source: Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, Vaccine Education Center
blurb: Vaccines for measles (1963), mumps (1967), and rubella (1969) were combined into one MMR vaccine by Dr. Maurice Hilleman in 1971.

headline: Poliomyelitis -- United States, Canada
source: CDC, Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
blurb: As of May 22, 1979, CDC reported four polio cases in Pennsylvania that year and suspected cases in two other states, most of them among Amish residents.

headline: Current Trends Childhood Immunization Initiative, United States -- 5-Year Follow-Up
source: CDC, Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
blurb: CDC looked back at the nationwide Childhood Immunization Initiative announced on April 6, 1977, which set a goal of vaccinating at least 90% of the nation's children by October 1979.

headline: TITLE III—VACCINE COMPENSATION
source: U.S. Statutes at Large, Public Law 99-660, 100 Stat. 3755 (govinfo.gov)
blurb: This part of a law approved on November 14, 1986, is the National Childhood Vaccine Injury Act of 1986, which added a new vaccine title to the Public Health Service Act.

headline: Recommendations of the Immunization Practices Advisory Committee Mumps Prevention
source: CDC, Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
blurb: A federal advisory committee issued mumps vaccine advice and noted that reported mumps cases rose from 2,982 in 1985 to 12,848 in 1987.

headline: Measles Prevention: Recommendations of the Immunization Practices Advisory Committee (ACIP)
source: CDC, Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
blurb: A federal advisory committee changed the routine childhood schedule from one dose to two doses of the combined measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine.

headline: Current Trends Measles --- United States, 1990
source: CDC, Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
blurb: Health departments reported 27,672 measles cases and 89 suspected measles deaths in the United States for 1990, up from 18,193 cases in 1989.

headline: About the Vaccines for Children (VFC) Program
source: CDC
blurb: Congress passed a law on August 10, 1993, that created the Vaccines for Children Program, which began on October 1, 1994, and provides vaccines at no cost to eligible children.

headline: Resurgence of Pertussis -- United States, 1993
source: CDC, Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
blurb: CDC reported 5,457 whooping cough cases in the first 48 weeks of 1993, the highest yearly number since 1967.

headline: International Notes Certification of Poliomyelitis Eradication -- the Americas, 1994
source: CDC, Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
blurb: On September 29, 1994, an international commission announced that the spread of wild polio virus had been stopped in the Americas.

headline: Notice to Readers Licensure of Inactivated Hepatitis A Vaccine and Recommendations for Use Among International Travelers
source: CDC, Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
blurb: In February 1995, the Food and Drug Administration licensed Havrix, a hepatitis A vaccine, for people age 2 and older.

headline: Pertussis Vaccination: Use of Acellular Pertussis Vaccines Among Infants and Young Children Recommendations of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP)
source: CDC, Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
blurb: A federal advisory committee recommended the newer DTaP vaccines for all five doses of the childhood schedule against diphtheria, tetanus, and whooping cough.

headline: Achievements in Public Health, 1900-1999 Impact of Vaccines Universally Recommended for Children -- United States, 1990-1998
source: CDC, Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
blurb: CDC looked back at the 1900s and compared reported cases of diseases such as measles, diphtheria, and whooping cough from early in the century with recent years.

headline: Measles --- United States, 2000
source: CDC, Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
blurb: CDC counted 86 confirmed measles cases in 2000, a record low at the time, and said the data suggest measles is no longer always present in the United States.

headline: Poliomyelitis Prevention in the United States
source: CDC, Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
blurb: As of January 1, 2000, a federal advisory committee recommended that children get only the injected polio vaccine (IPV), with the oral vaccine used only in limited cases.

headline: Achievements in Public Health: Elimination of Rubella and Congenital Rubella Syndrome --- United States, 1969--2004
source: CDC, Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
blurb: An independent panel that CDC brought together in October 2004 concluded that rubella is no longer constantly present in the United States.

headline: Preventing Tetanus, Diphtheria, and Pertussis Among Adolescents: Use of Tetanus Toxoid, Reduced Diphtheria Toxoid and Acellular Pertussis Vaccines Recommendations of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP)
source: CDC, Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
blurb: A federal advisory committee recommended that adolescents ages 11 to 18 get one dose of Tdap, a booster shot against tetanus, diphtheria, and whooping cough.

headline: Prevention of Hepatitis A Through Active or Passive Immunization: Recommendations of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP)
source: CDC, Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
blurb: A federal advisory committee recommended that all children get the hepatitis A vaccine at age 1.

headline: Update: Multistate Outbreak of Mumps --- United States, January 1--May 2, 2006
source: CDC, Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
blurb: Eleven states reported 2,597 mumps cases between January 1 and May 2, 2006, in an outbreak that began in Iowa in December 2005.

headline: U.S. Reports: Bruesewitz v. Wyeth, 562 U.S. 223 (2011).
source: Supreme Court of the United States (U.S. Reports, via Library of Congress)
blurb: In a case about a DTP vaccine, the Supreme Court ruled that the 1986 vaccine injury law blocks lawsuits that claim a vaccine was badly designed.

headline: Pertussis Epidemic — Washington, 2012
source: CDC, Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
blurb: Washington State declared a whooping cough epidemic on April 3, 2012, and by June 16 had 2,520 reported cases, the most in any year since 1942.

headline: Measles — United States, January 1–May 23, 2014
source: CDC, Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
blurb: CDC counted 288 confirmed measles cases from January 1 to May 23, 2014, more than the highest full-year total since measles was eliminated, which was 220 cases in 2011.

headline: Recommendation of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices for Use of a Third Dose of Mumps Virus–Containing Vaccine in Persons at Increased Risk for Mumps During an Outbreak
source: CDC, Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
blurb: A federal advisory committee recommended a third dose of mumps vaccine for people whom health officials identify as being at higher risk during a mumps outbreak.

headline: Increase in Hepatitis A Virus Infections — United States, 2013–2018
source: CDC, Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
blurb: Reports of hepatitis A infections in the United States rose 294% in 2016 through 2018 compared with 2013 through 2015.

headline: National Update on Measles Cases and Outbreaks — United States, January 1–October 1, 2019
source: CDC, Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
blurb: The United States had 1,249 reported measles cases from January through September 2019, the highest yearly number since 1992.

headline: Public Health Response to a Case of Paralytic Poliomyelitis in an Unvaccinated Person and Detection of Poliovirus in Wastewater — New York, June–August 2022
source: CDC, Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
blurb: Polio was confirmed in an unvaccinated adult in Rockland County, New York, and the virus was also found in wastewater in two nearby counties.

headline: 2024 Provisional Pertussis Surveillance Report
source: CDC
blurb: CDC's early count showed 35,435 reported whooping cough cases in the United States in 2024, compared with 7,063 in 2023.

headline: Measles Update — United States, January 1–April 17, 2025
source: CDC, Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
blurb: CDC counted 800 measles cases from January 1 to April 17, 2025, with 82% tied to an outbreak in New Mexico, Oklahoma, and Texas.

headline: Supreme Court Orders New Review of Religious Exemptions to School Vaccines
source: Education Week
blurb: The Supreme Court told a federal appeals court to take a second look at a challenge by Amish schools and parents to a New York law that ended religious exemptions from required school vaccinations.

headline: CDC Acts on Presidential Memorandum to Update Childhood Immunization Schedule
source: CDC Newsroom
blurb: CDC said it would sort childhood vaccines into three groups, and that vaccines for measles, mumps, rubella, polio, whooping cough, and diphtheria stay in the group recommended for all children.

headline: Update on the review of measles elimination status
source: Pan American Health Organization
blurb: The Pan American Health Organization said the review of whether the United States and Mexico still count as having eliminated measles will take place in November 2026.

headline: Measles Cases and Outbreaks
source: CDC
blurb: As of September 24, 2026, CDC had counted 3,659 confirmed measles cases in the United States in 2026.
